title: Zero-lot bungalow, link semi-D, guarded estate: what am I buying?
excerpt: Developers' names for landed homes can blur what you're getting. Sean explains zero-lot bungalows and link semi-Ds, what you can and can't do on individual title, and how strata estates are run.

question.context: After a first video on landed home types, viewers asked Sean what terms like zero-lot bungalow and link semi-D actually mean, and how individual-title and strata landed homes differ in daily life.
question.text: What do common landed home labels mean, and how do individual-title and strata estates differ in practice?

answer.quote: these are just languages of developers
answer.summary: A zero-lot bungalow is a semi-D with the pair pulled apart, and a link semi-D is a terrace house shaped to look like a semi-D. On individual title you own the land but can't close public roads, and renovations need council approval; on strata, a management body runs the estate and can enforce maintenance fees.

reasons.title: Names can oversell
reasons.body: A zero-lot bungalow has one side built on the boundary with no windows or doors, so only three sides open. A link semi-D is a link house with staggered fronts and small gaps that make it look semi-detached.

reasons.title: Individual title has public roads
reasons.body: The council maintains roads, lamps and drains, so residents can't simply gate them. They can register a residents' association, apply for a guarding licence, and collect fees, though some neighbours never pay.

reasons.title: Renovations still need approval
reasons.body: Building by-laws limit how far you extend to the front and back for fire safety. The council can fine owners, or order an unapproved extension torn down.

reasons.title: Strata estates are run by owners
reasons.body: A joint management body with the developer hands over to an owners' management committee. Under the Strata Management Act, owners who don't pay maintenance fees can face legal action.

actions: Ask exactly how many sides of a 'bungalow' have openings.
Check whether an estate's guarding is by a residents' association or a strata body.
Get council approval before extending an individual-title home.
For strata, confirm the development is registered as strata and use a licensed managing agent.
Join the management committee or attend its meetings.
caveat: Sean says foreigners can't buy individual-title landed homes, but rules for foreign buyers vary by state and price threshold; check the current ones.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this May 2018 follow-up to his first landed typology video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.
